desc:
Encoding. A singly linked list with n nodes is given by two arrays. The nodes are numbered 0..n-1; node 0 is the head, vals[i] is the value stored in node i and succ[i] is the number of the node after node i, or -1 if there is none. The node numbers say nothing about the order in the list: follow succ to find it.

The list has no cycle and contains all n nodes. For each node, consider the list that remains after deleting only that node (the others keep their order). Count the nodes for which the remaining list is a palindrome, i.e. reads the same from head to tail as from tail to head. An empty list counts as a palindrome. Two different nodes are counted separately even if they leave the same sequence of values.

Example: the list 1 -> 1 -> 2 -> 1 (vals = [1,1,2,1], succ = [1,2,3,-1]). Deleting the first or second node leaves 1, 2, 1 (a palindrome), deleting the node with value 2 leaves 1, 1, 1 (a palindrome), deleting the last node leaves 1, 1, 2 (not a palindrome). The answer is 3.
constraints: The list starting at node 0 visits all n nodes and ends at a node with succ = -1
hints: Trying every deletion costs O(n<sup>2</sup>) in total, which is fine for n = 4,000 in a compiled language but is not the idea. Think about which deletions can possibly work.

Deleting any node of a block of equal neighbouring values leaves the same sequence. So count whole blocks (maximal runs of equal values) rather than single nodes. Find the first pair of positions i < j that mirrors each other and holds different values.

If there is no such pair, the list is already a palindrome and the only deletions that keep it one are those inside the run of equal values around the centre. Otherwise only the run containing position i and the run containing position j can work: test each by checking the list without one element of that run, and add the length of the run when it works.
editorial: Read the values into an array a. Removing any element from a maximal run of equal values gives the same array, so it is enough to decide for one representative per run and then add the run length.

If a is not a palindrome, let (i, j), with j = n - 1 - i, be the outermost pair with a[i] != a[j]. All pairs outside it match. A deletion that fixes the list must remove an element equal to a[i] from the left part's run or an element equal to a[j] from the right part's run (any other deletion leaves the outer mismatch in place after the shift). So only the run of i and the run of j are candidates, and they are different runs because their values differ. For each candidate delete one element, test palindromicity in O(n), and add the run length if it succeeds.

If a is already a palindrome, a deletion keeps it a palindrome exactly when it removes one of the equal values around the centre: for odd n the run containing the middle element, for even n the run containing the two middle elements. Its length is the answer; for example [7] gives 1 (the empty list) and [2,2] gives 2. Everything is O(n) time and O(n) space for the array.
